called time-varying coefficient vector autoregression with external factors, specifically tailored for real-time analysis. A frequentist approach has been developed to estimate the time-varyning coefficients and their standard deviations, in addition to testing the significance of external factors and their lags. The model's specifications can be estimated using either historical or real-time information about external factors, and the framework supports both daily and monthly data series. The frequentist approach to testing the lags of external factors has been replaced with a block bootstrap method to address potential issues related to time-varying coefficients. The suitability and effectiveness of the proposed model have been demonstrated using both a real-world example and a simulated dataset. The results from a real-world example show that the Chinese monetary policy stance and its lags have a significant impact on Chinese exports, with the policy stance's effect varying over time. The results from a simulated dataset confirm the accuracy and power of the proposed testing methods.

groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet it's a critical step in maintaining the clarity of these graphs. We present an effective, adaptive strategy for pre-processing edge crossings before applying an optimization algorithm to reduce them. This approach involves removing crossings at the lowest possible cost within a limited area around the line representing the connection between the two sets of objects, and then applying an optimization algorithm such as the CRC (Crossing Reduction by Climbing) method to further reduce crossings. Our research includes a theoretical analysis of this technique's performance, as well as an assessment of its efficacy in comparison to other established methods following the application of various optimization algorithms to a variety of challenging scenarios, and it outperformed these alternatives in all cases.

It is then demonstrated that this $sR(n)$ algebra is equivalent to the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through application of quantum group theory. A key centralizer member is the integral part of a fraction involving variables $x,y$ where $n=x+y$. It is shown that various operators, including the Coxeter-Cartier operators, the braid operators, and the Kauffman operators, are represented within this $sR(n)$ algebra. A direct generator set is also established for the $sR(n)$ algebra, enabling the determination of its generator dimensions. Furthermore, a multiplicity-free decomposition of these generators is obtained, allowing for the calculation of the algebra's rank. The results are then applied to derive the generator dimensions and ranks of the $sR(n)$ algebra for various values of $n$.

To investigate this effect, we examined the relationship between star formation rates and galaxy bulge-to-total ratios using a large sample of galaxies observed by the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) in the COSMOS field. Our sample consists of 159 main sequence galaxies between redshifts 0.5 and 3. We found that the rate at which star formation occurs in galaxies decreases as the bulge-to-total ratio of the galaxy increases. We observed a significant decline in this rate by a factor of 10 when the bulge-to-total ratio of a galaxy doubles from 0.1 to 0.3. This decrease is not linear and occurs more rapidly at higher bulge-to-total ratios. We also discovered that the decline in star formation rate occurs primarily in the central regions of galaxies, with an enhanced rate of decline observed in the central regions of massive galaxies. Our findings are consistent with a model in which the growth of a galaxy's bulge suppresses star formation in the central regions of the galaxy. This effect becomes more pronounced in more massive galaxies, which experience more rapid bulge growth.

We discovered a significant deviation in the rotation curve of L1506, showing a slowdown at its center before picking up speed again. The same flow is also responsible for the formation of the CG30 dust pillar, as well as the shaping of the B1 outflow. The observed internal structure within the Perseus cloud demonstrates that it is not a simple, uniformly rotating sheet, but rather a complex, dynamically evolving system influenced by external flows and forces.

This research aims to address this issue by developing an innovative framework called NewsTrust that utilizes crowd-sourced truth-ratings to identify and eliminate false information on a real-time basis. The proposed system is based on a dynamic reputation management system that evaluates both the credibility of news sources and the accuracy of news articles. The proposed strategy focuses on a tiered reputation system that assesses both the overall reputation of a user and the reputation associated with a specific news article. The approach utilizes a set of novel metrics to evaluate the credibility of users and news articles, which include a user's overall reputation, the reputation of the user who posted the article, the reputation of the news source, and the reputation of other users who have rated the article. The research includes experimental results from a large-scale simulation that demonstrates the effectiveness of the NewsTrust system in reducing the spread of false information on social media platforms. Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area called the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this region, training them requires a large amount of data which can be hard to obtain for a new and emerging treatment like LITT. In response, this paper proposes an innovative framework called Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis, consisting of multiple stages to artificially create more training data with various characteristics, thereby enhancing the precision of the therapy evaluation. This approach outperformed existing image synthesis methods in both quantitative and qualitative assessments, demonstrating a significant improvement in defining the treated region in LITT patients, which can lead to more accurate evaluations and potentially more effective treatments.

Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, but none are universally effective for CV systems due to the variety of methods and the diversity of scenarios. We discuss the current state of research on linear-optical state reconstruction techniques, focusing on deterministic methods that rely on specific non-linear optical processes such as SPM, SA, PDC, and SPDC, as well as all-optical electronic reconstruction systems. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented three problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, these problems gained significance, and their variations became crucial to the development of metric geometry. Recently, T. Banach's student, K. Kuratowski, along with two of her colleagues, developed the theory of the Euclidean distance function, which proved effective in this context. They then employed this theory to provide straightforward proofs for the original problems proposed by Menger, as well as new, more complex variations. The document at hand serves as a compilation of Kuratowski's articles on this subject, which originally dispersed across various Polish journals. We have translated these articles from their Polish originals into English, ensuring that the text remains faithful to the original publications.

One area that has gained significant attention is the vulnerability to poisoning attacks in outsourcing training and machine learning services. In such attacks, an adversary manipulates the data used for training, with the aim of creating inaccurate models that can be exploited in the future. To address this issue, a variety of detection methods have been proposed to identify poisoned data in outsourcing training and machine learning services. However, these methods often rely on a centralized system with high computational capabilities, which may not be feasible in outsourcing training and machine learning services due to data privacy concerns. To address this limitation, an ensemble learning-based scheme called FedADC has been developed to detect poisoned data in outsourcing training and machine learning services. In this scheme, multiple detection methods are distributed across multiple clients, which then collaborate with each other to identify poisoned data. The results of our experiments conducted on various datasets demonstrate that the FedADC scheme is highly effective in detecting poisoned data, outperforming existing detection methods in outsourcing training and machine Learning services.

a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy to mitigate this issue is for nodes to share their local model updates with the server, rather than their raw data. However, this approach leaves nodes with limited incentive to cooperate, as they risk exposure to sensitive information within these updates. Furthermore, even if nodes are motivated to cooperate, they may lack the capability to create updates, particularly in the case of costly machine learning tasks such as regression. We propose a novel framework called Graph Neural Network-based Privacy-preserving Learning, which incorporates privacy and incentive mechanisms to facilitate learning on a graph. Within this framework, nodes can opt to share either their local model updates or the GNN layers associated with them, allowing for both the protection of sensitive information and the inclusion of costly machine learning tasks. We also design an optimized learning algorithm that accounts for the costs associated with sharing updates or GNN layers, as well as a consensus mechanism to incentivize nodes to cooperate. We further develop two specific applications of this framework: a generic method for learning any regression function and a specialized method for learning graph automorphism invariant functions. We demonstrate the efficacy of our framework through a series of experiments on both synthetic and real-world graphs, resulting in learning accurate models while keeping sensitive information private.

systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has led to the development of a sophisticated system capable of generating a vast amount of data. This data's massive volume, velocity, and variety create challenges in ensuring the system's safety, performance, and reliability. To address these challenges, a novel consensus-based learning approach for IoVs, called Vehicle Clustered Federated Learning (VCFL), has been proposed. This VCFL framework consists of multiple vehicle clusters, each with a local model, that contribute to a global model through consensus-based federated learning. The vehicle clusters' formation and the global model's update are optimized to achieve better performance, faster convergence, and higher accuracy. The VCFL framework's benefits and the consensus-based learning process's advantages can lead to improved vehicle safety and reduced risks of data breaches. However, this framework also introduces additional complexities and the risk of vehicle clusters' compromised behavior, which poses security threats to the system's integrity. To address these threats, a formal security analysis was conducted using the Tamarin protocol verifier, demonstrating the VCFL framework's resilience to various attacks. The results showed that the framework safeguards against manipulation, replication, and replay attacks but is vulnerable to a compromised cluster's actions. To further enhance security, an encryption mechanism was suggested, which can be implemented using Identity-Based Encryption (IBE) or Attribute-Based Encryption (ABE) to prevent unauthorized access and malicious behavior.

This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed, which significantly reduces model complexity without sacrificing accuracy. In addition to this optimized algorithm, a customized hardware platform is also designed to efficiently execute the FDHT-LSTM model by incorporating a sophisticated memory access scheme that minimizes data conflicts and allows for real-time matrix transformations. Experimental results indicate that the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the hardware accelerator exhibit high performance, outperforming existing compressed LSTM models by an order of magnitude in terms of model size while also demonstrating substantial improvements in accuracy across multiple video recognition datasets. Furthermore, the proposed FDHT-LSTM architecture is found to excel over a leading tensor decomposition hardware model in a real-world implementation on a chip set, achieving a remarkable 3.5 times increase in throughput and a 40% reduction in energy consumption on a representative video recognition task.

Although Bayes factors provide a framework for evaluating theories, they are not without their issues, particularly when analyzing complex data sets. One common problem is the time required to compute Bayes factors, which can be substantial even with moderate-sized data sets. Furthermore, with increasing data set sizes, the accuracy of Bayes factors in estimating the relative fit of models also degrades. To address these challenges, we propose a new approach that calculates the difference in Bayes factors directly, skipping the necessity of computing the Bayes factors for each model individually. This method is particularly effective for comparing two models, as it bypasses the need to perform multiple Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) iterations or bridge sampling, which can be particularly beneficial when analyzing large data sets. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach using a simulation study and a real-world example from the cognitive sciences, showing that it offers a faster and more accurate alternative to existing methods for assessing model fit through Bayes factor differences.

in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. A Convolutional Neural Network was trained on an initial snapshot of a dark matter simulation, with the goal of predicting halo masses at a given point in time, in a similar manner to the formation of halos through gravitational collapse. the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results were found to match the experimental data reported in a previous study. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while for the dimer, significant impacts were noticed. For both the monolayer and the bilayer Nb films with an incorporated Mn dimer, the closure of the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov gap was predicted. Additionally, the closure of the YSR state energy gap in the presence of a dimer was found to occur at a critical exchange field, which was calculated to be around 10 millitesla for the monolayer film and around 15 millitesla for the bilayer film.

This problem hinders the detector's ability to accurately measure the vertex region and consequently impacts its overall precision. To address this challenge, a proposal is made to incur precision impairments on the incoming lepton detector science before the vertex detector, which would then compensate for these effects in measurement and analysis. This pre-impacted detector would essentially serve as a proxy for the affected area and enable the accurate reconstruction of scattering vertices. This concept is particularly relevant for the proposed MATHUSLA experiment, which aims to detect fleeting particle phenomena by imaging decay patterns on a two-dimensional plane.

We develop a new method, called the "repertoire" of invariant manifolds, which assesses the preservation of invariance as system parameters are altered. The repertoire consists of closed sets that contain the invariant manifolds of interest, measured through a precise topological metric. We then explore the practical implementation of this methodology, detailing an automated script that can be used in MATLAB to visualize and analyze invariant manifolds. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we apply the "repertoire" method to three distinct nonlinear systems, analyzing their invariant manifolds as their parameters are varied.

The uniqueness solution to this problem was established in a previous study. Here, we work towards a reconstruction strategy for the initial heat distribution. A formula derived from the PDE's energy estimate can be used to represent the reconstruction in the form of an operator. Integrating this operator, we can reconstruct the initial heat distribution from the measurements. The image's real part corresponds to the reconstruction of interest, while the image's imaginary part is instrumental in ensuring the reconstruction's uniqueness. Validation of this approach and the overall uniqueness of the reconstruction strategy was achieved by developing an integral equation that bonds the reconstruction's real and imaginary parts at the point of interest.

By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillation lengths. Here, the "atmospheric" mass scale is directly produced at tree-level, whereas the "solar" scale arises through radiative processes, mediated by the dark sector. Furthermore, we determine the parameter ranges that meet theoretical requirements, in addition to dark matter relic abundance and direct detection standards. Utilizing two-loop renormalization group equations, we assess the stability of the vacuum and verify the consistency of the inherent dark parity symmetry. Consequently, we derive a minimum threshold for the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude.
